Notebook.Title: Sia Essentials: From Components to Reactive Systems

Section.Title: How this notebook is organized
Section.Paragraph: Sia is an entity-component-system framework. A World owns lightweight Entity handles; components describe data; queries select component shapes; systems process those selections. Every cell in this notebook is an independent program: press Run on any lesson and only that lesson compiles and runs — jump around, break one on purpose, and the others won't notice. Lessons that build on the same component types each declare their own copies. The alternative — cells sharing a scope, where one run replays the earlier cells first — is what Example 1 demonstrates.

The notebook host already provides a fresh variable named world. Keep the data flow explicit: direct component access is the low-level path, while generated Views and Commands mutate data and notify interested systems. Every cell is editable — change a number, break something on purpose, press Run again. Nothing here can touch anything outside its own disposable World.

Section.Title: 1. World, entities, components, and generated Views
Section.Paragraph: Components are ordinary structs. HList.From creates an entity with a known component shape. Adding [Sia] to component fields generates a typed View plus change events such as Position.SetX. The View is the default mutation API when observers must react.
That last line goes to a second view instead of the console — Notebook.Render is the same mechanic Example 1 introduced.

Section.Title: 2. Queries, matchers, systems, and stages
Section.Paragraph: activeMovers and MovementSystem's own matcher are two independent values that happen to both exclude Disabled — nothing ties them together. Building the same matcher in two places means keeping them in sync is on you; a matcher belongs to whoever asks the question, not to a component type.

MovementSystem favors clarity here: entity.Get<Velocity>() for a read, Position.View for a write that should notify observers. When a hot loop has nothing to notify, skip the View: query.ForSlice((ref Position p, ref Velocity v) => { p.X += v.X; p.Y += v.Y; }) iterates the same contiguous component storage the View wraps, with no per-field event dispatch at all. Reach for it once profiling says the dispatch overhead matters, not by default.

Section.Title: 3. Events make systems reactive
Section.Paragraph: The matcher says which entities a system can see; the trigger says when it needs to run. This system observes only generated position-change events. Setting through Position.View changes the data first, then dispatches the event that wakes the system on its next tick.

PositionChangedSystem ticks every frame regardless, but its query only ever contains entities whose SetX/SetY fired since the last tick — an entity that matches the matcher but never raised the trigger stays invisible to Execute forever. The trigger, not the matcher, decides who shows up.

Section.Title: 4. Bundles and Commands express intent
Section.Paragraph: A generated [SiaBundle] groups a reusable component shape. A Command is both executable behavior and an event: it updates through the World, and event-driven systems can observe the same intent without coupling to the caller.

A Command is exactly the intent it says it is and no more — Damage subtracts, full stop, with nothing here stopping Health from going negative if the amount is large enough. A DeathSystem that watches Health drop to zero would be a second, separate piece added on top, not something Damage owes you for free.

Section.Title: 5. Addons hold world-scoped services
Section.Paragraph: Addons are services whose lifecycle belongs to a World. AcquireAddon returns the existing instance or constructs and initializes one; RemoveAddon runs its cleanup hook. This keeps service ownership explicit without a global container.

AcquireAddon hands back the same live instance on every call until the addon is actually removed — "clock initialized" prints exactly once per lifetime here, no matter how many times AcquireAddon<TutorialClock>() gets called before that.

That's the whole application loop: create data, select it with matchers, tick ordered systems, mutate through Views or Commands, and keep long-lived services in addons. One more piece ties it together — how systems get ordered into a chain and re-run frame after frame.

Section.Title: 6. Composing system chains
Section.Paragraph: SystemChain.Empty.Add<T>() builds an ordered pipeline; CreateStage(world) turns it into a SystemStage you Tick() once per frame — call Tick() again and the whole chain runs again, in the same order, against whatever the world looks like now. The same system class can appear more than once in one chain: pass a factory to Add<T> and each instance gets its own constructor arguments and its own private state.

Two systems, two ticks: SpawnWaveSystem ran four times total, each time with whichever constructor arguments its instance was built with. The census bars in the Render pane are just that entity count grouped by name prefix and drawn as text — nothing about Render requires a graphical surface.
The next notebook builds higher-level composition — reactors, reactive reconciliation, events that can be intercepted, and safe concurrency — on top of these same primitives.
